know: The book's claim: the answer a payment API returns is the first of several promises, kept over days by parties that cannot see each other, and a payment is done when it is settled and every record of it agrees.

How the book states evidence: six kinds of statement, the year in every sentence about Stripe or Adyen, the evidence-age flag, the words 'Not public', and the 'Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ' table in every chapter of Parts I to VIII.
The names of the sixteen failure patterns and their four families: money truth, integration, trust, platform and scale.

Larkfield in outline: a fictional studio-software platform with 6,200 studios and €1.12 billion of member payments in 2026, split by studio between Stripe and Adyen, nine systems named by role, eight incidents (seven of them in 2026), and the 2027 Keel program with its decisions K1 to K8.
believe: A payment failure is usually a promise that some system recorded as the truth, and the remedy is on the integrator's side of the provider's API: keys, states, ledger entries, reconciliation and named owners.
A sentence about how Stripe or Adyen works is worth what its source and its date are worth, and 'Not public' is an answer, not an omission.
can_do: Name the pattern and the family behind a described payment incident.
Recognize a Larkfield incident or a Keel decision (K1 to K8) when a later chapter cites it by name.
Say of a sentence in the book whether it is a documented fact with a date, industry practice, a labeled inference, a recommendation, a Larkfield illustration or an assumption.
Go from the decision in front of them to the chapter that answers it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one of the four pages.
Each page's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.
A reader who has read only the preface can say what the Double Charge was, which named pattern it is an instance of, and what Larkfield decided about it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only the preface pages: what was the Double Charge at Larkfield, which of the sixteen patterns and which family is it, and which Keel decision answers it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: On 1 November 2026, during the first-of-month renewals, a provider call timed out and the renewal job retried with a new idempotency key (the identifier that lets a provider recognize a repeated request); 1,840 members were charged twice, €71,300 was refunded and 212 disputes followed anyway. The Double Charge, in the money truth family. K1, one writer, one key: every money-moving call goes through the payment service and its key is derived from the business event (for a renewal, membership id plus billing period plus the number of the scheduled attempt), never generated per network call.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Chapter 1 can rely on the preface for what its audience already knows: after the preface a reader recalls at least twelve of the sixteen pattern names and at least five of the eight incidents without looking back.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Without looking back: list as many of the sixteen failure patterns and of Larkfield's eight incidents of 2025–2026 as you can, by name.
acceptance_criteria.expected: At least twelve pattern names and at least five incident names, with no invented ones.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader who has read only the preface reads a 'Where They Differ' table row the preface does not contain correctly: which cells are documented, what 'Not public' means and whose reading the last column is.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A later chapter's 'Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ' table has a row whose Stripe cell cites a 2017 engineering post with the note '(Evidence age: 9 years; the current system may differ)', whose Adyen cell says 'Not public', and whose last column says one design 'suggests' a priority. Using only the preface: what may you conclude about Stripe today, about Adyen, and about the last column?
acceptance_criteria.expected: About Stripe: what the company said it built in 2017, which may have been replaced; it is not a statement about the current system unless current documentation confirms it. About Adyen: the public record the author searched does not say; it does not mean Adyen lacks the mechanism or does it differently. The last column is the author's inference, not a documented fact about either company.

thesis.question: What does the book argue, how far can its statements about Stripe and Adyen be trusted, how do payment systems fail, and which company do its examples come from?
thesis.claim: The book argues that the answer a payment API returns is the first of several promises, kept over days by parties that cannot see each other; it states about Stripe and Adyen only what a dated public source says, and marks the rest as inference or as not public; payment systems fail in sixteen recurring patterns, each of which records a promise as the truth or leaves a dependency on the provider untested; and its examples come from one fictional platform, Larkfield, whose eight incidents of 2025–2026 were all decided on its own side of the provider's API.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a provider's API has already solved payments, so that a success response means the money has moved, an incident is the provider's fault or a bug in one service, a platform with eight incidents should change provider, and how Stripe or Adyen works inside is known well enough from their engineering blogs to be stated without dates.
thesis.so_what: A reader who accepts this starts every later chapter with three questions (which promise is this, who made it, which record proves it was kept), checks the year on every sentence about a provider before relying on it, and reads Larkfield's decision to keep both providers and change its own keys, records and ownership as the consequence of the argument, not as a compromise.
thesis.how_why: An authorization is the issuing bank's promise, clearing and settlement move the money days later through networks the integrator never sees, and a dispute can reverse it months afterwards; the integrator's systems learn of each step only through responses, webhooks and reports that can be late, missing or repeated. The public record has the same shape of gaps: Stripe's best-known posts on idempotency, rate limiting and versioning date from 2017, Adyen's account of its accounting system from 2021, and neither company publishes how its webhook sender is built or how one of its data centers takes over from another. The failures recur as patterns because each starts from a shortcut that matches how a provider's API behaves on the first day (a call returns success, a webhook arrives once) and that the slow parts of a payment contradict only later. At Larkfield the Double Charge came from a retry sent with a new key, not from the timeout that preceded it.

supporting_claims.claim: The answer a payment API returns is the first of several promises kept over days by parties that cannot see each other, and each major component of payment infrastructure exists to close the gap between that answer and the settled truth without losing or duplicating money.

Every statement the book makes about Stripe or Adyen is a documented fact with its year, a labeled inference or the words 'Not public', and the reader can tell which from the wording alone, in the prose and in each chapter's 'Where They Differ' table.

Payment systems fail in sixteen recurring patterns in four families, each begun as a shortcut that matched how the provider's API behaved on the first day, and the patterns chain: an integration, trust or scale pattern starts the chain and a money-truth pattern is where it is noticed.

One platform shows the patterns together: each of Larkfield's eight incidents of 2025–2026 was decided on its own side of the provider's API, so its Keel program changes its own keys, records, pacing and ownership and adds neither a provider nor an orchestration product.

role.contribution: Performs the journal's opening, states how the book handles evidence about Stripe and Adyen, and names the failure patterns and the running example every chapter refers to.

additional_patterns.applies_to: introduction to meet-larkfield: the claim about every payment, then the recurring ways payment systems fail, then one platform

flow.rationale: Each page supplies what the next one uses. The introduction gives the promise claim, the evidence labels and Larkfield in a few paragraphs; the patterns page needs all three, because it explains each pattern as a promise recorded as the truth, illustrates it with a Larkfield incident labeled as fiction, and separates that illustration from what a provider documents. The Larkfield page labels each of its eight incidents with a pattern name and each Keel decision with the pattern it answers, so it needs the patterns first. With the Larkfield page second, its incident table would carry pattern names the reader has not met; with the patterns page first, the reader would meet sixteen failures before knowing what a promise is in this book or which of the page's examples are fiction. The evolution page stands between the introduction and the patterns because it explains, in plain words, where the parties, records and delays came from; placed after the patterns it would explain failures the reader had already been asked to accept, and placed before the introduction it would be a history without the claim it serves.

hook.content: At 19:42 on Tuesday 9 March 2027, Mila Janssen buys a ten-class pass for €120 in a studio's app and sees 'Payment successful' two seconds later. At that moment no money has moved: her bank has made a promise, and the studio will be paid on Thursday, by systems that never saw her tap the button.

opening.bridge: From the developer's side, where a payment is one API call that returns success, to the provider's side, where that answer is the first of several promises kept over days by parties that cannot see each other.
opening.roadmap: This page gives the argument, the organization of the book and how to read its evidence about Stripe and Adyen; the next page walks from cash to today's layers; the third names the sixteen failure patterns; the fourth introduces Larkfield and the recurring payment; Part I then follows Mila's payment party by party.

closing.synthesis: The claim, the patterns and the platform are one argument at three sizes, and the walk from cash to code explains where the gap between a promise and its keeping came from: Larkfield's eight incidents are instances of the named patterns, each pattern is a promise recorded as the truth or a dependency left untested, and the Keel decisions (a key per business event, the provider's record as the truth, a ledger entry per movement, a rehearsed switch) are the book's claim written as a program. None of the three pages says alone that the same reading discipline applies to the providers themselves: what Larkfield experiences is illustration, and only a dated source is evidence.
closing.so_what: The reader can treat every chapter's opening scene as a view of one known landscape and one known list of failures, and can expect each chapter to explain a mechanism that closes the gap between an answer and the truth, with the evidence for how Stripe and Adyen build it kept apart from the fiction.
closing.callback: Mila's €120 class pass from the introduction's first paragraph, which returns on the Larkfield page as the recurring payment with its fixed figures: approved at 19:42 on Tuesday 9 March 2027, a €2.53 fee, €117.47 for Studio Noord, paid out on Thursday 11 March.

takeaway.content: Begin Part I by following Mila's €120 through every party it touches, and ask at each step who has promised what, who holds the money and which record says so.

posts.title: Introduction: Why Payment Infrastructure Is Hard
posts.question: What does this book argue, who is it for, and how should its evidence about Stripe and Adyen be read?

know: The book's claim and the timeline behind it: an authorization is a promise by the customer's bank, a capture is a claim, clearing and settlement move the money days later, a payout moves it again, and a dispute can take it back months afterwards.
How the book is laid out: four preface pages, ten parts from how money moves to how Stripe and Adyen chose to build, and four reference pages.

The six kinds of statement (documented fact, industry practice, labeled inference, recommendation, Larkfield illustration, assumption), the evidence-age flag for sources older than about three years, and the three tiers of take-away (established, depends on context, the author's synthesis).
How a 'Stripe and Adyen: Where They Differ' table is built: per aspect, what each company has documented with its year or the words 'Not public', and a last column that is the author's inference.

The asymmetry of the public record: Adyen is listed and publishes audited accounts; Stripe is private and publishes volume and customer counts in annual letters but no revenue; much of the best-known material on Stripe's API internals dates from 2017; neither company publishes its webhook delivery design, its card-vault internals beyond a paragraph, or where its systems run more finely than a continent or country (Adyen) or beyond two countries named for login and identity data (Stripe names no cloud region).
Larkfield and Mila's class pass in a few paragraphs, and the names of the sixteen failure patterns as a list grouped by family that the patterns page unpacks.
What the book leaves to its sibling books: reconciliation and posting from the finance side (RECONCILED) and payments as a merchant's order system sees them (ORDERED).
believe: The API's answer is not the outcome: a payment is done when it is settled and every record of it agrees.
Stripe and Adyen are the anchors because both publish enough to compare, not because either is the right answer for every business.
An honest 'Not public' is more useful to a builder than a confident guess about a provider's internals.
can_do: Go from the decision in front of them to the chapter to start with.
Tell a documented fact from an inference, a Larkfield illustration and an assumption when a chapter states one, and say how much a dated source supports about the present.
Read a 'Where They Differ' row and say which cells are evidence and which is the author's reading.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can state the book's argument and list the subjects of its parts in order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what does this book argue, and what will its parts cover, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The instant answer a payment API returns is not the truth but the first of several promises kept over days, and the architecture exists to close that gap without losing or duplicating money; then how money moves, getting a payment approved, ledgers and money movement, the API, trust (card data, fraud, authentication, compliance), billing and revenue, platforms, scale and reliability, four end-to-end journeys, and the Stripe and Adyen bets.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a decision the page's routing table lists, the reader names the chapter to start with.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your nightly job that charges customers timed out halfway, and you do not know which customers were charged. Using only this page: which chapter do you open first, and why not the reliability chapter?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The idempotency and retries chapter (Part IV), because the question is how to make a charge safe to send twice when the outcome is unknown; the webhooks and state-machine chapters follow for learning the true state. Reliability concerns keeping the path up, not what to do after an unknown outcome.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given four sentences in the book's style, the reader labels each with the kind of statement it is.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page, say what kind of statement each is and how far you may rely on it: (a) 'Adyen's Annual Report 2025 reports processed volume of €1,394.3 billion.' (b) 'INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED: a provider plausibly keeps slow webhook endpoints in a separate queue.' (c) 'Larkfield processed €1.12 billion for its studios in 2026.' (d) 'Assume the provider's cost on this payment is €0.61.'
acceptance_criteria.expected: (a) a documented fact with its source and year; it is the company's own figure under its own definition and is not revenue. (b) a reference-architecture inference by the author, not a fact about any company. (c) an illustration: Larkfield is fictional, so this is evidence about nothing. (d) an assumption for teaching, not to be used as a benchmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what the public record does and does not contain for the two companies, without overstating either.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: a colleague wants to compare Stripe's and Adyen's revenue and then copy 'how Stripe implements idempotency' from its engineering blog. What does this page tell you about each plan?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Revenue cannot be compared from public sources: Adyen is listed and reports net revenue in audited accounts; Stripe is private and publishes volume and customer counts but no revenue, and each company's volume figure has its own definition, so they are not ranked. The idempotency material is from 2017, about nine years old: it shows what Stripe said it built then; the book flags its age and checks it against current documentation, and how Stripe stores keys today is not public (Adyen described a distributed database for them in 2021).

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the page's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this page discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Who the book is for; the argument that a payment is a promise that takes days to keep; how the book is organized in ten parts; how to read the evidence labels, the take-away tiers and the 'Where They Differ' sections, and why Stripe and Adyen are the anchors; the fictional platform Larkfield and the recurring payment; how to find a chapter for a decision and what is left to the sibling books. Evidence: one fictional payment, and dated public facts about what the two companies publish.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the page, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: What does this book argue, who is it for, and how should its evidence about Stripe and Adyen be read?
thesis.claim: This book argues that the answer a payment API returns in two seconds is the first of several promises, kept over days by parties that cannot see each other and reversible for months, and that each component of payment infrastructure exists to close that gap without losing or duplicating money. It is for engineers and architects new to payments, and it states about Stripe and Adyen only what a public source with a date says, marking everything else as inference, illustration, assumption or 'Not public'.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that payments are a solved commodity behind an API, so that a newcomer should begin with a provider's quickstart and a feature comparison, and that what the two companies' engineering blogs describe can be taken as how their systems work today.
thesis.so_what: A reader who accepts this stops treating the API response as the outcome, asks of every design which promise it records and what will prove the promise was kept, and discounts any account of a provider's internals, including this book's, by the age and kind of its source.
thesis.how_why: Mila's €120 is approved at 19:42 on a Tuesday and reaches the studio on Thursday; between the two, the issuer, the network, the acquirer and the provider each act on their own records, and the integrator hears of it through responses, webhooks and reports. The companies publish unevenly: Adyen files audited annual accounts, Stripe publishes annual letters with volume but no revenue; Stripe's posts on idempotency, rate limiting and API versioning are from 2017 and Adyen's on its accounting system from 2021; neither publishes how its webhook sender is built or the topology and timing of a failover between its data centers or regions. A book that hid those gaps would teach invented internals, so each chapter shows per aspect what is documented, with its year, and what is not.

role.contribution: Performs the journal's and the part's opening: states the claim, the reading order and the evidence rules, explains the 'Where They Differ' sections, and gives the pattern names and Larkfield in outline so the next two pages have something to unpack.

posts.title: From Cash to Code: How Paying Got This Complicated
posts.question: How did paying for something, which was once settled on the spot with cash, come to involve so many parties, records and delays?

know: The steps by which payment moved from cash settled on the spot to today's layered infrastructure, and the concept each step introduced: credit and the record of a debt, the check and clearing, the card and its guarantee, the card network and its four parties, authorization at a distance, the payment provider, stored credentials and recurring charges, and the platform that stands between payer and seller.

For each step, both sides of it: what it made possible that could not happen before (a sale to a customer with no money until payday, to a stranger, to someone far away, to someone not present at all, by a seller too small to arrange card acceptance), and what it cost (a new party, a new delay, a new copy of a record or a new way to be cheated).
believe: Each step was a good bargain for buyer and seller alike: it opened trade that the earlier way of paying could not carry, and its cost was accepted for that reason. No step was ever removed, so today's complexity is the sum of those bargains, not a design.
Given those layers, the failure patterns of the next page are what one should expect, not signs of careless engineering.
can_do: Given a term from a later chapter (clearing, acquirer, authorization, chargeback, token, payment facilitator), say which step of the walk introduced it and what limit it answered.
Given a failure pattern's name, say which layer makes it possible.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader new to payments can say, for a concept the page introduces, which step brought it in and what limit of the earlier way of paying it answered.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: when a shop accepts a card from a stranger, why does it need an 'authorization', and what earlier way of paying did not need one?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The shop cannot know the stranger or the stranger's bank, so before handing over the goods it asks, through the network, whether the cardholder's bank will stand behind the payment; that answer is the authorization, a promise made in seconds while the money moves days later. Cash needed none because payment and goods changed hands at the same moment, and shop credit needed none because the shopkeeper knew the customer.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader can connect a failure pattern to the layer that makes it possible.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: paying a shop twice for one purchase is impossible with cash handed over a counter. Which later steps made it possible, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Paying at a distance through messages: the request and its answer travel separately from the money, so an answer can be lost and the request sent again, and the money moves later on someone else's record. The page ties this to the pattern it names for it (the Double Charge).

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every dated fact on the page has a source the style guide accepts, the page says once that it is a simplified account that follows the ideas, and it attributes no motives to companies or networks.
Every term is given in plain words before it is named, and no step uses a concept a later step introduces.
A reader can say, for a step of the walk, what it made possible for the seller and for the buyer as well as what it cost.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: when a shopkeeper sells bread on a promise to be paid on payday, who gains what, and who risks what?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The buyer gets bread now that they could not otherwise buy until payday; the shopkeeper makes a sale and keeps a customer who might otherwise go elsewhere or go without. The shopkeeper carries the risk that the customer never pays and that the notebook is wrong.

thesis.question: How did paying for something, which was once settled on the spot with cash, come to involve so many parties, records and delays?
thesis.claim: Paying became complicated one good bargain at a time: each new way to pay (credit at the shop, the check, the card, the card network, payment at a distance, the stored card, the platform) made possible a sale that could not happen before, to the gain of buyer and seller alike, and paid for it with a promise, a party to keep it, a record of it and a delay before it is kept; no earlier step was ever taken away, so a payment today carries all of them at once.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that payment systems are complicated because they are old, badly designed or protected by incumbents, so that a clean redesign, or a new technology, would make paying simple again.
thesis.so_what: A reader who sees each step as a bargain that both sides wanted stops looking for the one simplification that removes them, expects a failure wherever a promise and its keeping are separated, and reads the sixteen patterns of the next page as the price of what the steps made possible.
thesis.how_why: With cash, goods and payment change hands at once and nothing is left open, but only people who are in the same place and have the money now can trade. Every later step lets more people trade (the customer who is paid next week, the stranger, the buyer far away, the subscriber who is not there, the seller too small to deal with a bank) by separating goods and payment a little further, in distance, in time or in who is involved. Each separation is bridged by a promise that someone records and someone else must later honor. A promise can be forgotten, made twice, broken or forged, and each step added its own way for that to happen; the dates and institutions on the page are a small set of sourced anchors, and the account is a simplification that follows the ideas.

role.contribution: Explains, before the failure patterns are named, where the parties, records and delays behind a payment came from, what each of them made possible and what it cost, and introduces in plain words the vocabulary Part I then teaches properly.

transition_in.carries_over: The introduction's claim that the answer a payment API returns is the first of several promises kept over days by parties that cannot see each other.
transition_in.introduces: Where those promises and parties came from: the walk from cash to today's layers, one need and one concept at a time.

posts.title: Paid Twice, Paid Never: Sixteen Ways Payment Systems Go Wrong
posts.question: In which recurring ways do payment systems fail, and what do the failures have in common?

know: The sixteen pattern names, each with its warning sign and its family.

What each family points to: money truth, a record of money that nothing outside the system has confirmed; integration, an assumption about the provider's interface that was never tested; trust, a control over card data, fraud or verification handed to the provider and then not watched; platform and scale, a dependency, a peak or a regulated role nobody rehearsed or named.
How the patterns chain, and that a chain is usually noticed at a money-truth pattern and started elsewhere.
believe: A pattern accumulates from decisions that were each reasonable when they were made, so finding it is not finding someone to blame.
Repairing the money at the end of a chain (refunding, re-sending a payout) does not hold; changing the assumption at its start does, and that change is rarely a new provider.
can_do: Name the pattern and family behind a described incident, the upstream pattern to check for, and the chapter that addresses it.
Ask for the number or record that would confirm a warning sign.
Use the patterns as questions in a design review, an incident review and a provider evaluation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a described incident the page does not contain, the reader names the pattern, its family, the upstream pattern to check first and the remedy direction.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A tutoring marketplace marks a lesson as paid when the checkout page redirects back to it with a success parameter. A month later finance finds 300 delivered lessons whose bank-transfer payments never arrived. Using only this page: which pattern is this, which family is it in, which upstream pattern would you check for, and what is the remedy direction?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The Phantom Payment, money truth family: the system believed a payment succeeded without the provider's confirmed record saying so. Upstream, check for A Card by Any Other Name (integration family): a bank transfer was assumed to be final at the redirect, as a card approval appears to be. Remedy direction: take the payment's state from the provider's record, not from the browser, and model when each payment method becomes final.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say, for each of the four families, where it tells them to look.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: name the four families of patterns and say in one clause each what kind of thing has gone wrong.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Money truth: a record of money that nothing outside the system has confirmed. Integration: an assumption about the provider's interface (delivery, versions, payment-method behavior) that was never tested. Trust: a control over card data, fraud or verification handed to the provider and then not watched. Platform and scale: a dependency, a peak or a regulated role that nobody rehearsed or named.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a warning sign, the reader names a number or record to ask for before concluding the pattern is present.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A colleague says 'we have a Black-Box Balance'. Using only this page: what would you ask to see before agreeing?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A breakdown of the provider balance on one date into payments, fees, refunds, disputes and reserves, set against the company's own ledger for the same date, with the size and age of the difference nobody can explain.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every Larkfield example can be followed without the Larkfield page and is not mistaken for evidence: each is labeled fictional, names its systems by role with a one-clause explanation, and attributes no undocumented behavior to Stripe or Adyen.
A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the page's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this page discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Sixteen named patterns in four families (money truth, integration, trust, platform and scale), each with a typical quote, what it looks like, why it happens, what it costs, a Larkfield illustration, a remedy direction and the chapters that address it; then how the patterns chain and how to use them in a review. Evidence: invented examples from a fictional platform, and dated provider documentation where a provider's behavior is stated.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the page, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: In which recurring ways do payment systems fail, and what do the failures have in common?
thesis.claim: Payment systems fail in sixteen recurring patterns in four families: a record of money that nothing outside the system has confirmed; an assumption about the provider's interface that was never tested; a control over card data, fraud or verification handed to the provider and then not watched; a dependency, a peak or a regulated role nobody rehearsed or named. Each began as a shortcut that matched how the provider's API behaved on the first day, and they chain: the money-truth patterns are where a failure is noticed, and one of the other eleven is usually where it started.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that each payment incident is a separate bug in the service that showed the symptom or an outage at the provider, to be fixed in that service, compensated with refunds, or avoided by moving to a different provider.
thesis.so_what: Faced with a double charge, a missing payout or an unexplained balance, the reader names the pattern, follows its chain upstream to the retry rule, webhook assumption, unwatched deadline or untested peak that started it, and assigns an owner there; a correction made only to the money will have to be made again next month.
thesis.how_why: Every shortcut matches how the provider's API looks on the first day: a call returns success, a webhook arrives once and in order, a card behaves like every other method, verification is a form filled in at sign-up. The slow parts of a payment contradict each of these only later and only sometimes, so the shortcut survives testing and fails under a timeout, a peak or a rule change. At Larkfield the first-of-month renewal peak met a timed-out call and a retry that generated a new key, and 1,840 members paid twice; an expired certificate on a webhook receiver stopped events for nine hours, and 3,200 memberships were shown as unpaid. In both, the money error was the last link.

role.contribution: Gives the book its shared names for failure: without it Larkfield's incidents are eight anecdotes and no chapter can open by naming the patterns it works on.

transition_in.carries_over: The layers of the previous page: each way of paying added a promise, a party, a record and a delay, and none was removed; together with the introduction's claim that a payment failure is a promise some system recorded as the truth, and its rule that Larkfield is illustration and never evidence about a provider.
transition_in.introduces: What those layers make possible: sixteen recurring failure patterns, each unpacked with a typical quote, what it looks like, why it happens, what it costs, a Larkfield illustration, a remedy direction and the chapters that address it; then the chains the patterns form and how to use them in a review.

posts.title: Meet Larkfield
posts.question: Which company do the book's examples come from, why does it run on both Stripe and Adyen, and what state are its payment systems in?

know: Larkfield at a glance: a fictional Rotterdam software platform for independent fitness and wellness studios, founded in 2017, with 6,200 studios in five countries, 2.9 million active members, €1.12 billion of member payments in 31.4 million payments and €46.0 million of revenue in 2026, and a payments team of 11.

Why it has two providers and how a payment is assigned: Stripe since 2017 (44% of 2026 volume), Adyen since 2024 (56%), split by studio and not by payment, with 1,140 studios on Stripe online and Adyen terminals at the front desk; Larkfield never holds member funds and is not the seller.
The January 2027 landscape: nine systems named by role, from the booking app and the payment service to the ledger, the webhook receivers and the reconciliation job, and no orchestration product.
The eight incidents of 2025–2026 by name, each with its pattern and cost, and the eight Keel decisions K1 to K8.
Mila's €120 class pass and the five other recurring examples, whose amounts and dates do not change between chapters.
believe: Larkfield's problems are on its own side of the provider's API: in each of the eight incidents, what Larkfield's own code, forms or processes did decided the outcome.
Keeping both providers and adding no orchestration product follows from what failed; the providers are not what failed.
Nothing that happens to Larkfield is evidence about Stripe or Adyen.
can_do: Follow any chapter's opening scene without a re-introduction of the company, its people or its systems.
Look up a figure, a person, an incident or a Keel decision when a chapter cites it.
Explain an incident as a named pattern acting on this landscape.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can explain why Larkfield runs on two providers, how a payment is assigned to one, and why Keel adds neither a provider nor an orchestration product.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: why does Larkfield use both Stripe and Adyen, what decides which provider a given member payment goes to, and why does the Keel program not consolidate on one provider or buy an orchestration product?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Stripe since 2017 for Larkfield's own subscriptions (Billing) and member payments (Connect); Adyen since 2024 for in-person payments on one platform with online and for local acquiring in the Netherlands and Germany. The studio decides: a studio is on one provider for online payments, and all front-desk terminals are on Adyen. The eight incidents were decided by Larkfield's own keys, receivers, forms, pacing and reminders, so Keel changes those (K1 to K7) and makes the existing second provider a rehearsed switch for online card payments (K8) without adding a product.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given the name of an incident and of a Keel decision, the reader says what each is without help from the citing chapter.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A later chapter mentions 'the Silent Webhook' and 'K2'. Using only this page: what was the first, which pattern is it, and what does the second change?
acceptance_criteria.expected: On 14 September 2026 the TLS certificate of Larkfield's Stripe webhook receiver expired shortly after midnight on Monday; events failed for 9 hours, 3,200 memberships were shown as unpaid and members were turned away at check-in on Monday morning; no money was lost, 460 support tickets. The Trusted Doorbell. K2: the provider's record is the truth and the webhook is the doorbell; receivers verify, persist and acknowledge, a state change is confirmed against the provider's own record (the payment object where the API allows reading it, the settlement report where it does not), and a job sweeps everything still pending.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what the eight incidents have in common and what that implies for the providers.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: what do Larkfield's eight incidents of 2025–2026 have in common, and what do they tell you about Stripe or Adyen?
acceptance_criteria.expected: In each, the outcome was decided on Larkfield's side of the provider's API: a retry with a new key, an expired certificate, an unverified bank-details form, a pinned API version, a public widget with no limit, an unpaced renewal job, a reminder sent to an unmonitored address, a ledger not reconciled to the providers' balances. They tell you nothing about Stripe or Adyen: Larkfield is fictional, and a provider's behavior is established only by a cited source.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every system and payments term on the page is explained in one clause where it first appears, so the page can be read before Part I.
A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the page's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this page discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The company, its business lines and figures; why it runs on two providers; its systems in January 2027; its people; the eight incidents; the Keel program; the recurring payment and the other worked examples; how the chapters use it. Evidence: invented but consistent figures in reference tables, no public sources, and nothing to be read as a statement about Stripe or Adyen.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the page, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.

thesis.question: Which company do the book's examples come from, why does it run on both Stripe and Adyen, and what state are its payment systems in?
thesis.claim: The examples come from Larkfield, a fictional studio-software platform that moved €1.12 billion in 31.4 million payments in 2026 through two providers, split by studio: Stripe since 2017, and Adyen since 2024, added to take in-person payments on the same platform as online ones and to acquire locally in the Netherlands and Germany. Its eight incidents of 2025–2026 share one cause: in each, Larkfield's own code, form or process treated a provider's answer, event or deadline as settled. Its 2027 program, Keel, therefore changes its own keys, records, pacing and ownership, keeps both providers and adds no orchestration product.
thesis.disputed_by: The reading that a platform with double charges, bounced payouts and frozen sellers on two providers has a provider problem or a two-provider problem, and should consolidate on one provider or put an orchestration product in front of both.
thesis.so_what: The reader can take each chapter's scene as one more view of a single landscape, check any figure against this page, and ask of each Keel decision what the equivalent change would be in their own integration before asking whether their provider is the right one.
thesis.how_why: Each system was added for the need of its year: a Stripe integration in 2017 with a webhook receiver that predates everything built later, a payment service with an adapter per provider for the Adyen launch in 2024, a small ledger in 2025 after the first unexplained difference. The joins between them were never designed as a whole, so the renewal job could mint a new idempotency key on a retry, the billing integration stayed outside the payments team, and the nightly reconciliation covered one provider only. A second provider or a routing product changes none of those.

role.contribution: Supplies the one platform, with fixed figures, incidents, decisions and recurring payments, that every chapter's scene and worked example draws on, and performs the part's closing.

transition_in.carries_over: The sixteen pattern names, and the Larkfield incidents the patterns page used one at a time as illustrations.
transition_in.introduces: The platform as a whole: its business lines and figures, its two providers, its systems and people, the eight incidents as one landscape's history, the Keel decisions and the recurring payments.
